title: The House of God
note:
Built from the four curriculum photographs in Drive’s “01 - Curriculum Source” for Primary / Chapter 05 and the memory-verse page in “06 - Memory Verse”: the opener (p.25), the lesson (pp.26–27), the questions (p.27), the colouring page (p.29) and the close (p.30).

**This chapter has the same printed title as Primary Chapter 2.** The book calls both of them “THE HOUSE OF GOD” — Chapter 2 on p.13 over St. Luke 2: 41 - 52, and this one on p.25 over St. Luke 15: 11 - 24, which is the prodigal son. The title here is the book’s and is kept, because inventing a different one is not this importer’s job. The *slug* is `the-lost-son`, from the father’s own closing words, because a slug is a route and two chapters cannot share one.

**That leaves two cards on the Primary shelf reading “The House of God”, which is a real problem for a child and needs an editorial decision.** The options are to leave it as the book has it, to disambiguate on the shelf, or to ask the Samajam which title was intended. Flagged rather than silently resolved.

**No artwork yet.** “04 - Story Artwork” is empty, so the story is twenty-two text cards and nothing carries a picture.

p.26 carries the teacher’s pen marks — three bracketed sections numbered 1, 2, 3 — lining up with the three questions. A reading aid, not an answer key; every answer below is quoted from the printed lesson.

The book’s “Colour the picture” on p.29 sets a pencil activity, which has no game here.

story.text: There was a man who had two sons.
The younger one asked his father for his share.
His father was sad, but divided his property between them.
A few days later the younger son sold his share.
He left home with the money and went to a far country.
There he wasted it all with his friends in wild living.
Then a great famine came, and he had nothing left.
His friends left him.
He went to work for a farmer, who sent him to look after pigs.
He was so hungry he could have eaten the pigs’ food.
But no one gave him anything.
Then he started thinking.
At his father’s house even the workers had more than enough to eat.
He decided to go home and say he had sinned.
So he set out for his father.
While he was still far from home, his father saw him.
He felt sorry for him. He ran, put his arms round him, and kissed him.
The son said he was no longer worthy to be called his son.
But his father called for the best robe, a ring and shoes.
He arranged a grand feast.
He said, “This son of mine was dead and is alive again.”
“He was lost and is found.”

curriculum.source: Primary Mar Thoma Vol-1, Chapter 05 “THE HOUSE OF GOD”, p.27 — “ANSWER THE QUESTIONS”
curriculum.note: Transcribed from the curriculum photographs, read at full size. Three questions and no “Mark it as Right or Wrong”. Every answer is quoted from the printed lesson on pp.26–27.

questions.question: What did the younger son demand from his father?
questions.objective: Know that he asked for his share of the property.
questions.answer: His share. “The younger one asked his father for his share. His father was sad but divided his property between his two sons.” (p.26)

questions.question: How did the younger son lose everything?
questions.objective: Know the chain: he sold up, went far away, wasted it in wild living, and then famine came.
questions.answer: He spent it. “the younger son sold his property and left home with the money. He went to a far off country and wasted all his money with his friends in wild living.” Then “there was a great famine in that country, and he had nothing with him.” (p.26)

questions.question: How did the father receive the son when he came back?
questions.objective: Know that the father ran to him and held a feast rather than punishing him.
questions.answer: He ran to him. “his father saw him and felt sorry for him. He ran, put his arms around his son, and kissed him.” Then the best robe, a ring, shoes and a grand feast. (pp.26–27)

games.title: The Asking
games.objective: Know that the younger son asked for his share of the property.

interactions.prompt: What did the younger son ask for?
interactions.hint: His father divided the property in two.

options.label: A ring and the best robe

games.note: Question 1, and the one choosing game this band allows in four. All four options are things that really happen in this lesson — the robe and ring, the feast, the pigs — so the question is answered by remembering which one he *asked* for, rather than by spotting the invented option.

games.title: How It Went
games.objective: Put the losing in order, so the famine arrives after the money is already gone.

interactions.hint: The famine came after the money was gone.

items.label: He left for a far country
He fed pigs and went hungry

games.note: Question 2. The lesson's answer is not one fact but a slide with an order to it, and the order is the point: the famine arrives *after* the money is gone, so it is what exposed him rather than what ruined him. The planner grouped this with question 1 into a single sequence; they are separated here because asking for the money and losing it are two different things a child should be able to tell apart.

games.title: Coming Home
games.objective: Follow what the father did — saw, pitied, ran, embraced, and feasted — rather than what he might have done.

interactions.prompt: Turn over how his father met him.

items.label: His father saw him far off
He called for the best robe

games.note: Question 3. A `reveal`, because the answer is a run of five things the father did and the force of it is cumulative — he saw, he pitied, he ran, he embraced, he feasted. A quiz would make a child pick one of them and call the rest wrong.

games.title: True or Not?
games.objective: Hold what the son said and what the father said — the two speeches the questions do not ask about.

interactions.prompt: Say what you think. Then we will look.

statements.source: The father was angry and sent his son away again.
statements.ask: Did the father send his son away again?
statements.because: No. He ran, put his arms around his son, and kissed him.

statements.source: I am no longer worthy to be called your son.
statements.ask: Did the son say he was no longer worthy?
statements.because: Yes. He said, “I am no longer worthy to be called your son.”

statements.source: He arranged for a grand feast.
statements.ask: Was there a feast when he came home?
statements.because: Yes. His father arranged for a grand feast.

statements.source: For this son of mine was dead and is alive again; he was lost and is found.
statements.ask: Did the father call him lost and then found?
statements.because: Yes. He said, “he was lost and is found.”

games.note:
The fourth game, written by hand because the book asks three questions and the Primary band wants four to five. Primary Chapters 1 and 4 did the same.

What it covers is the two speeches the questions skip: what the son had decided to say, and what the father said over him. Statement 1 is written from a false sentence, so its `ask` keeps that polarity and the honest answer stays “no”.

verse.text: I will set out and go back to my father and say to him: Father, I have sinned against heaven and against you. I am no longer worthy to be called your son.

practice.hint: It is what he decided to say before he set out.
words: I will set out and go back to my father
Father, I have sinned against heaven and against you.
I am no longer worthy to be called your son.
practice.note: Stage 1, phrase ordering, cut by hand rather than by the agent. Its Primary rung cuts on word counts and produced “Father, I have sinned against heaven and” / “against you.” — a join in the middle of a phrase. These four pieces break where the sentences do. The build checks they spell the verse exactly.

practice.prompt: I will set out and go back to my ______
practice.hint: He is going to the one person he wronged.
practice.note: Stage 2, the missing word with the sentence whole around it. “Home” is the near miss worth having — true of the story, and not the word the verse uses.

practice.prompt: I am no longer ______ to be called your son.
practice.hint: One word, and it is what he believes he has lost.
practice.note: Stage 3, the right-hand side taken away. The word carries the whole of what he has understood about himself, which is why it is the one worth supplying from memory.

practice.hint: A journey, a greeting, and two things he admits.
words: and go back to my father
practice.note: Stage 4, full reconstruction — seven pieces where stage 1 had four.

practice.prompt: Where does our verse come from?
practice.hint: It is inside this chapter’s own Bible portion.
practice.note: Stage 5, the reference chosen against near misses. All three are inside this chapter’s own portion, St. Luke 15: 11 - 24 — 11 is where it begins and 24 is where it ends.

verse.note:
Read from p.30 through the Memory Verse agent: `--fetch --source-dir` over the curriculum photographs and the memory-verse page, the supervised read, then `--from-extraction`. That page lives in “06 - Memory Verse” rather than with the lesson, which is this class’s arrangement.

Five stages in the shape Primary Chapters 2, 3 and 4 use. **Stage 1 was cut by hand** — see its own note.

The reference is printed “St. Luke 15: 18,19a”, with the comma and the “a”, and is kept exactly so: the verse stops partway through verse 19.

Translation is unresolved: p.30 does not name one.

No second opinion — the teacher’s editorial Sheet was not available for this run.

decision.statement: I will repent and ask God for forgiveness of my sins. He will forgive.
decision.note: The curriculum’s own My Decision from p.30, first person and unchanged.

song.note: The four lines of the Song on p.30, in the Latin script the book prints them in. Not translated and not completed.

prayer.text: Father, forgive me whenever I drift away from You. Hold me close to You Amen.
prayer.note: The closing Prayer from p.30, word for word — including “Hold me close to You Amen.”, which the book prints without a stop before the Amen. The chapter also opens with a prayer on p.25: “Forgiving Lord, we come to You. Cleanse and bless us. Amen.”

celebration.message: He was lost and is found. His father ran to meet him.
celebration.note: The father’s own words from p.27, which are the point of the whole parable.
